Article Title: US court sentences Nikhil Gupta to nearly 20 years for plot to kill Pannun
Article Text:
Indian national Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 235 months in US prison over foiled assassination plot against designated terrorist Pannun

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A US court in New York on Friday sentenced Nikhil Gupta, an Indian citizen, to 235 months, roughly 19 and a half years, in prison over his role in a foiled plot to assassinate designated terrorist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun on American soil.US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the punishment after Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in Feb to murder-for-hire, murder-for-hire conspiracy, and money-laundering conspiracy.The judge indicated that Gupta will likely face deportation or removal once he completes his prison term.Federal prosecutors alleged that an Indian govt official recruited Gupta in 2023 to arrange the killing of Pannun, a US citizen known for advocating secession from India. Court filings stated that Gupta passed along Pannun's personal details and helped organise an advance payment to someone Gupta believed was a hitman, who turned out to be an undercover US law enforcement officer. The defence counsel argued Gupta was not the mastermind and asked the court to punish him solely for his own conduct.Prosecutors maintained the case involved a serious attempt to silence political speech inside the United States.The US state department had asked for 24 years of imprisonment for Gupta.However, Gupta's counsel had requested a reduced sentence, of 12 years, while submitting a remorse letter to the judge ahead of his sentencing on Nov 20. They had requested the judge to consider the probation department's recommendation of a similar duration jail term, besides Gupta pleading guilty and not wasting the court's time.The prosecutors had, however, asked to consider his act of planning a murder on foreign soil as brazen and asked for maximum sentence to "send a message".Gupta has claimed to be a victim of deception and that he was promised by an individual to settle cases in exchange for plotting the killing.
Article Summary: Indian national Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 235 months in US prison over foiled assassination plot against designated terrorist Pannun. US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the punishment after Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in Feb. The judge indicated that Gupta will likely face deportation or removal once he completes his prison term.

Article Title: The brighter a city glows, the more its economy reveals: The story of luminosity index
Article Text:
How satellite night-time lights help researchers track economic growth, urbanisation and regional development.

Decoding night time lights

How satellites count light

India’s night time lights

India’s state economies: What night lights can tell us

India’s glow-getter stats

Maharashtra GSVA vs Nightlight

Maharashtra's night-time light growth closely tracks changes in modified GSVA growth, with both showing a sharp decline in 2020 and a subsequent recovery.

Gujarat GSVA vs Nightlight

Gujarat's night-time light growth shows sharp fluctuations alongside economic activity.

Karnataka GSVA vs Nightlight

Karnataka's night-time light growth broadly tracks modified GSVA trends, including a sharp pandemic-era dip and recovery.

Nightlight across nations

South Korea and North Korea’s light divide (Credit: Nasa)

Algeria’s oil and gas fields emit significant night-time lights. (Credit: WorldBankBlogs)

Morocco's map of nighttime lights (Credit: Datapartnership)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

So, can we trust the lights?

After dark, cities become constellations.Roads trace bright lines, factories glow through the night, and neighbourhoods gather like stars against the black. Seen from space, streetlights, vehicle headlights and tube lights shining through windows can make the city look like a sky turned upside down.But this glowing pattern is more than a pretty picture!Researchers study these lights for clues about where human and economic activity is growing, slowing or shifting. They are often called night-time lights or night-time luminosity. The term luminosity index may sound like one official score, but there is no single global index that ranks how well every economy is doing.Instead, satellites record the brightness of different places. Researchers group those readings by area and compare them with economic data. The result can serve as a proxy, a rough indicator, for activity that is difficult to measure quickly or in detail.The concept has been tested over different countries through the years.The IMF has used night-time lights to show the contrast between North and South Korea. In Algeria, the World Bank used them to track economic activity while official figures lagged.Gaurav S Ghosh, associate partner at Grant Thornton Bharat told TOI that night time light offers an interesting measure of economic activity. The luminosity index “has been used recently to proxy economic performance with some credibility.”He further added that other measures might include e-way bill volumes, vehicle registrations, and other transportation indicators.You may ask, why lights?Homes, shops, roads, factories and transport hubs all leave a glow after sunset. A town’s expanding halo of light may point to new buildings, more businesses or better access to electricity. But brighter lights do not automatically mean people are better off or the economy is stronger.While a satellite can capture the glow, it cannot tell what made it. A bright patch could come from a busy factory, a stadium or a new housing colony. Night-time lights show researchers where to look; other data helps explain what they find.A satellite doesn’t see a city as one glowing spot. It divides the Earth’s surface into tiny squares, or pixels, and records how bright each patch is.Researchers first clean up the readings by filtering out things that can affect the picture, such as clouds, moonlight, snow and firelight. They then add up or average the brightness recorded across an area, such as a district or state. Comparing these readings over time can show whether a place is getting brighter or its lit-up area is spreading.The readings also depend on the satellite being used. Some capture more detail than others, so researchers account for these differences before comparing data across places or years. The RBI’s October 2026 study, for example, used NASA’s Black Marble data, which is adjusted for moonlight and the atmosphere. The study discussed two satellite systems: the older DMSP/OLS, which collected annual readings from 1992 to 2013, and VIIRS, which has operated since 2011 and captures light in greater detail.Researchers then check whether changes in night-time light move alongside changes in official economic figures. If they do, the readings can help estimate activity while official numbers are still being prepared.But satellites only record brightness. They cannot tell whether a new patch of light comes from a factory, a shopping area or a brightly lit road. Researchers need other data to understand what the glow means.India gets a GDP update every quarter. State economies are harder to track: official figures for Gross State Value Added (GSVA), the value of goods and services produced in a state, are generally released once a year and can arrive 12 to 18 months later. That leaves a long gap before policymakers get a detailed picture of how each state is doing.To see whether newer data could help fill that gap, RBI researchers studied Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka. They combined satellite readings of night-time lights with Google Trends data, which shows how often people search online for different topics.The two sources offer different clues. Night-time lights show where illumination is changing, while searches related to jobs, shopping, travel and property can reflect what people are looking for. Researchers combined these signals with past GSVA figures to estimate current state-level activity before official data became available.In tests, the model using both night lights and Google search trends produced smaller forecast errors than a model relying on past GSVA figures alone. The reduction was about 38% for Maharashtra, 54% for Karnataka and nearly 62% for Gujarat. The improvement varied by state, and the results apply to the study’s model and test period.The findings are promising, but they do not mean satellite data can replace official state figures. They only suggest that combining different signals may help produce a more timely estimate while statisticians work on the official numbers.Nasa’s night-time image of the Korean Peninsula offers a striking example of what satellite lights can reveal. South Korea glows with cities of different sizes, while much of North Korea appears dark. Pyongyang and Yangdŏk show up as small clusters; Seoul is the brightest. The image highlights differences in population and urban development, but it cannot explain on its own why an area is dark or how much its residents earn.Algeria offers a different lesson: why researchers always need to separate certain sources of light before using them to track the wider economy. Oil and gas sites can be unusually bright at night, so their glow could distort the picture if mixed with lights from towns and businesses.In a World Bank analysis, researchers separated the two.They found that lights from gas flaring, burning off gas during oil production, helped explain 94% of monthly crude oil production levels. For non-hydrocarbon activity, night lights in four regions covering about 80% of Algeria’s population explained 87% of non-hydrocarbon GDP levels. That share rose to 93% after researchers accounted for trends and seasonal changes.Night lights can also help show what happens after a sudden shock. After the 2023 earthquake in Morocco, a World Bank-supported project tracked changes in brightness across the country and in areas hit by the quake. The team used satellite data that had been adjusted for clouds and stray light, including moonlight. In that project, brighter readings meant more light, not a direct count of businesses, jobs or money lost.The ADB looked at the Philippines and compared night lights with official figures on household spending, poverty and population. At the regional level, brighter places tended to have higher household spending. The link was weaker when researchers looked at smaller provincial areas. And when they compared changes in lights with changes in poverty or spending over time, the results were less clear.To an extent, yes,Night-time lights can offer a timely clue, but they need context. Luminosity index can give researchers a detailed, up-to-date clue, particularly when official economic figures are delayed.But the glow can come from many sources, and its link to economic activity varies from place to place. A brighter area, for instance, could reflect new streetlights or infrastructure; it does not automatically mean more jobs or higher incomes.That is why the luminosity index works best alongside official statistics and other data. It can help flag where activity may be changing, but it cannot explain the change or show on its own whether people’s lives are improving.The lights can point researchers towards the story, other evidence helps fill in the details.
Article Summary: Satellites record the brightness of different places. Researchers group readings by area and compare them with economic data. The result can serve as a proxy, a rough indicator, for activity that is difficult to measure quickly or in detail. Night-time lights show researchers where to look; other data helps explain what they find.

Article Title: India vs US interest rates: Trump cites 'look at India' example to turn up heat on Fed
Article Text:
Trump compares US interest rates with India

India vs US: How do their GDP growth rates compare?

Why are the Fed and RBI following different interest rate policies?

Trump calls for lowest interest rates in US

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump on Friday criticised the Federal Reserve over its interest rate policy, citing India's economic growth as an example of how lower borrowing costs could support expansion. He argued that the US economy could achieve growth of 15-20% if the central bank reduced interest rates.Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump accused the Federal Reserve of being "very political" and alleged that it raised borrowing costs whenever the US announced strong economic figures, rather than lowering rates to support further growth."Interest rates are too high because we have a very political Fed. I'm not blaming the chairman, but the fact that we have a very political Fed. Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the interest rates. They do that for a reason. It should be the opposite," Trump said.He argued that strong economic performance should allow the central bank to reduce interest rates because better economic indicators reflected improved creditworthiness. Trump also claimed that the Fed's approach was restricting America's economic potential."We do just the opposite. We do it to destroy the country. When we have these great numbers, you shouldn't keep raising the rates. You should lower rates because we're a better credit. We would have a GDP of 15 or 20 per cent, not 4 per cent. We'd pay off the debt very rapidly. That's the way it should work. But we do it in reverse," he said.Drawing a comparison with India, Trump pointed to the country's economic growth and monetary policy, arguing that the US could achieve a much higher growth rate if borrowing costs were reduced."If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP. We'd have a 14%, 15%, maybe even a 20% GDP. It's really a sad thing when you do so great and then they (Fed) raise the interest rate. The fact is, we've blown through it," the US President said.However, the latest official monetary policy figures show that India's benchmark interest rate is higher than that of the US.According to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) October 7 monetary policy decision, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) increased the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%. The standing deposit facility rate was set at 5.25%, while the marginal standing facility rate and bank rate were raised to 5.75%.In comparison, the US Federal Reserve maintained its federal funds target range at 3.75%-4% in its October 28 policy decision.This means India's benchmark repo rate is 1.50 to 1.75 percentage points higher than the US federal funds target range. The two rates are not identical instruments, but they provide a broad comparison of the monetary policy benchmarks in the two economies.Also Read| Beyond Nvidia: Inside 7 decades of the US-China spy war India's latest official GDP data also provides context to Trump's reference to the country's economic performance.According to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), India's real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in the first quarter of the financial year 2026-27, covering April to June 2026.In the US, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that real GDP expanded at an annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026, covering July to September. This followed growth of 2.2% in the second quarter.However, the two growth figures use different measurement periods and conventions. India's 7.8% represents year-on-year growth, while the US figure of 3.4% is a seasonally adjusted annualised quarterly growth rate.The figures therefore provide an indication of the two economies' recent performance but are not directly comparable without adjusting for these differences.The difference in interest rates reflects the distinct economic conditions and monetary policy priorities of the two countries.The Federal Reserve operates under a dual mandate of achieving maximum employment and maintaining price stability. Its long-term inflation target is 2%.According to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 3.6% year-on-year in September 2026. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased 3.1%.Both measures remained above the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target, providing an important consideration for its monetary policy decisions.In India, the RBI's monetary policy framework focuses on maintaining price stability while keeping growth objectives in mind. The central bank's inflation target is 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%.The RBI's October decision to increase the repo rate by 25 basis points also reflected its assessment of inflationary risks and broader economic conditions.Trump further argued that the US should have the lowest interest rates globally, citing its position in the international economy and its contribution to the financial success of other countries.Explaining his position, he said, "We're the country that makes other countries successful. Some of them are considered financial elite, but they are not. They are only elite because of us. So we should have the lowest."Trump has repeatedly criticised the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, arguing that high borrowing costs restrict economic expansion and increase the government's debt-servicing burden.However, the central bank's decisions are based on its assessment of inflation, employment and broader economic conditions, rather than GDP growth alone.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump criticised the Federal Reserve over its interest rate policy. He argued that the US economy could achieve growth of 15-20% if the central bank reduced interest rates. The difference in interest rates reflects the distinct economic conditions in the two countries.

Article Title: Anthropic shares crash 13% a day after record IPO as retail investors face losses
Article Text:
Anthropic’s IPO opens retail access to Claude’s parent company, but investors face limited allocations, uncertain opening prices and risks from early volatility.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Retail investors who rushed to buy Anthropic shares following its initial public offering (IPO) faced losses on Friday as the stock plunged 13%, reversing much of its gains on the first day of trading.The shares, which opened at $112 on Thursday against an IPO price of $83, closed at $97 before falling to $85 by 12:20 pm ET (1720 GMT) on Friday, according to LSEG data.The sharp decline came after retail investors recorded more than $750 million in Anthropic share transactions on Thursday, marking the highest turnover for a stock debut in Vanda Research's records. The figure surpassed the $670 million recorded for SpaceX during its IPO in June.Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 apiece on Thursday in what the report described as the biggest IPO in history, giving public market investors their first opportunity to invest in a leading artificial intelligence company.The strong retail interest also resulted in the third-largest day of net retail buying for a stock on its debut in records dating back to 2012, according to Vanda Research. However, net buying remained below the records set by SpaceX, at $118 million, and Coinbase, at $92 million."Different investors are different but most will be willing to look through the short-term volatility and focus on the bigger future," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda, said of Anthropic.Anthropic said that less than 20% of its shares were allocated to retail investors. A person involved in the offering said the allocation was slightly lower than initially expected because of strong demand from institutional investors.In the United Kingdom, around 3.6 million shares worth approximately $300 million were allocated to retail investors, according to RetailBook, which coordinated the offering.British investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown said its clients received 34% of the shares they had requested, in line with allocations made through other platforms.A European retail investment platform said Anthropic's trading volume, number of traders and average order size on its first day were lower than those recorded for SpaceX.The decline in Anthropic shares coincided with a broader fall in global stocks on Friday as investor sentiment towards artificial intelligence weakened.Investors are increasingly seeking stronger returns from the massive investments being made in AI model training, computing infrastructure and data centre expansion.The concerns have raised questions about whether companies investing heavily in artificial intelligence will be able to generate sufficient returns to justify their expenditure.Anthropic and SpaceX have reserved a larger share of their IPO offerings for retail investors, with SpaceX allocating around 20% to smaller investors.Traditionally, IPO allocations have favoured institutional investors, with a 90:10 split between institutional and retail investors, according to Fidelity.
Article Summary: Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $83 apiece on Thursday in what the report described as the biggest IPO in history. Retail investors recorded more than $750 million in Anthropic share transactions on Thursday, marking the highest turnover for a stock debut in Vanda Research's records.

Article Title: GTA 6 makes history with $3.8 billion in first-day sales, biggest entertainment launch ever
Article Text:
GTA 6 breaks entertainment industry record with $3.8 billion in opening-day sales

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

“Grand Theft Auto VI” generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day, setting a record for the biggest launch of any entertainment product in history, publisher Rockstar Games said on Friday, as the latest instalment in the blockbuster franchise recorded unprecedented demand after 13 years.The figure was based on the company’s estimates of global sales through the end of Thursday, the day the game was released. Rockstar also said it had sold 32.5 million units before launch, setting a record across platforms.“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a release.The launch substantially surpassed the opening performance of its predecessor, “Grand Theft Auto V”, which was released in 2013. According to Rockstar’s figures, the earlier game generated around $800 million in its first 24 hours, while it took three days to reach $1 billion in retail sales.“GTA V” went on to become one of the best-selling video games of all time. Publisher Take-Two Interactive has said it accounted for more than 230 million of the franchise’s over 470 million units sold worldwide.The $3.79 billion opening also exceeded the approximately $2.9 billion worldwide box-office collection of “Avengers: Endgame”, which regained its position as the highest-grossing film after a re-release.Earlier on Friday, market research firm Sensor Tower estimated that “GTA VI” had generated $2.36 billion in revenue from approximately 24.6 million units sold. Rockstar’s later announcement was based on its own estimates of worldwide first-day retail sales.The game went on sale on Thursday for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with its release beginning in New Zealand and rolling out across markets at midnight local time. PlayStation had earlier said it was working with Rockstar to allow players to preload the title nine days before launch, following record pre-orders on its digital store.Set in Vice City, a fictionalised version of Miami in the state of Leonida, the game follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval as they navigate crime and attempts to improve their circumstances. Rockstar spent more than eight years developing the title and delayed its release twice.The game has also received eight nominations for the Game Awards, scheduled for December 10.
Article Summary: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day. It is the biggest launch of any entertainment product in history, publisher Rockstar Games said. The latest instalment in the blockbuster franchise recorded unprecedented demand after 13 years. Rockstar also said it had sold 32.5 million units before launch.

Article Title: AI sell-off batters Wall Street; S&P 500 enters correction, Nasdaq turns negative for year
Article Text:
Wall Street major plunge in Friday's session

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wall Street stocks tumbled on Friday as a sharp sell-off in technology and artificial intelligence-related shares intensified, pushing the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year and sending the S&P 500 into correction territory.The S&P 500 plunged 3.7 per cent to 6,910.39, its steepest weekly decline in more than 18 months. The index has now fallen more than 10 per cent from its October 6 record high, meeting the technical definition of a market correction. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28 per cent to 22,617.73, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 1.93 per cent to 48,147.33.The sell-off extended across global markets, with Japan's Nikkei falling 5.06 per cent and South Korea's Kospi losing more than 5 per cent. Taiwan's stock market fell 17 per cent for the week, its biggest weekly decline since 1990. MSCI's global equities gauge shed 8.1 per cent over the week, its steepest drop since early 2020.Chipmakers bore the brunt of Friday's selling. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 10.7 per cent, while shares of AMD, Micron Technology and Broadcom dropped 13.3 per cent, 13.9 per cent and 12.2 per cent, respectively. Nvidia fell 14 per cent, extending its decline to nine sessions out of the past 10.The pressure reflects growing investor concerns over the high valuations of AI companies, the scale of spending on data centres and whether future earnings will justify the investments. Nvidia has also faced company-specific scrutiny, including a US securities regulator's investigation into its accounting practices and concerns linked to its business dealings with a Singapore-based firm investigated over suspected chip shipments to China."Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, adding that strong AI demand and successful stock listings were no longer enough to sustain investor appetite amid questions over valuations, borrowing costs and corporate profitability.Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, also came under pressure in its first full day of trading after its high-profile market debut. Its shares fell 9.1 per cent to $88.30, after dropping as much as 14.5 per cent during the session. The stock remained above its initial public offering price of $83, but was well below its brief peak of $115.10 on Thursday.As investors moved away from riskier assets, US government bonds rallied. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note fell more than 10 basis points to around 4.95 per cent, marking its biggest daily decline since October 22.The 30-year yield also fell, while the two-year yield dropped more than 13 basis points.In commodities, oil prices rose amid concerns over possible attacks linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran and continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude settled around $92.61 a barrel, up 0.68 per cent, while US crude gained 1.49 per cent to $83.67.Gold and silver, meanwhile, extended their losses. Spot gold fell 2.81 per cent to $3,520.09 an ounce, its lowest level in 14 months, while silver dropped 4.22 per cent to $40.95.
Article Summary: The S&P 500 plunged 3.7 per cent to 6,910.39, its steepest weekly decline in more than 18 months. The index has now fallen more than 10 per cent from its October 6 record high, meeting the technical definition of a market correction. The sell-off extended across global markets, with Japan's Nikkei falling 5.06 per cent and South Korea's Kospi losing more than 5 per cent.

Article Title: US market regulator probes issues in Nvidia's accounting practices: Report
Article Text:
Nvidia faces fresh US regulatory scrutiny over accounting and Singapore revenue disclosures, as per reports

Mounting legal and regulatory pressure

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, with enforcement staff scrutinising potential accounting issues at the chipmaker, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. The probe adds to mounting pressure on the company, which is already facing scrutiny over its business links to a Singapore-based firm investigated for suspected shipments of AI chips to China.The investigation, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is focused on potential accounting issues, the two people said. The probe comes amid renewed scrutiny of Nvidia's accounting disclosures, particularly its reporting of revenue from Singapore.Last year, Nvidia changed its method of reporting geographic revenue, using customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses. The company said the change would provide a more accurate picture of its revenue distribution, but Singapore was subsequently removed from its geographical breakdown.The Financial Times, citing company accounts, reported this week that Nvidia made the change even as sales in Singapore had surged to almost half of its global revenue.The issue has drawn attention amid investigations into possible shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China through Southeast Asia, which has emerged as a hub for suspected chip-smuggling activity following US export restrictions.US authorities have been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed since 2024 over possible export-control violations involving alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week. Megaspeed was historically a large Nvidia customer and was led by Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. China has denied the allegation. The company has said Alice Huang left in August 2025 and that it conducted "lawful business".The SEC's inquiry comes as investors raise questions about complex financing arrangements across the AI industry. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers and provided guarantees linked to data-centre projects using its equipment.Critics say such arrangements could make it harder for investors to assess the quality of reported revenue and companies' financial exposure. SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock told Reuters last month that the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure investors receive a full picture of potential risks.On Tuesday's earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company would be more selective about financing deals across the AI industry.The accounting probe is the latest challenge for Nvidia, whose shares have been hit by a wider scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, alongside the investigation into Megaspeed.The Justice Department is also reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion proposed acquisition of open-source platform Hugging Face as part of a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and business practices, Reuters reported last month.Nvidia shares fell about 13 per cent on Friday after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe, extending losses from an earlier decline of more than 6%.The SEC under President Donald Trump has said it will focus on traditional securities violations, including accounting fraud. It recently created a financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division to develop cases involving accounting and auditing practices.
Article Summary: US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices. Investigation is focused on potential accounting issues, two people said. Probe comes amid renewed scrutiny of Nvidia's revenue disclosures. Nvidia changed its method of reporting geographic revenue, using customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses.

Article Title: 'Pee on your brain, rip your heart out': How Jensen Huang 'tortured' employees repeatedly
Article Text:
A new report details allegations of repeated humiliation, verbal abuse and threats against employees by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Public humiliation and threats at workplace

Complaints over management style date back to 2005

Employees divided over Huang's leadership

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang repeatedly humiliated and threatened employees during his tenure at the chipmaker, using violent language and public put-downs as part of his management style, a New York Times report said on Friday. The report, citing current and former employees, detailed incidents spanning nearly two decades, including threats to physically harm subordinates and insults directed at them during company meetings.Huang had spoken about his approach to management during a fireside chat two years ago. “I’d rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,” he said.The accounts offer details of the management culture at Nvidia, which Huang transformed from a graphics-chip business into a major player in the artificial intelligence industry over 33 years.According to the report, Huang regularly reprimanded managers in front of their teams. In one instance, he went around a room and told managers he would kill them, a person familiar with the incident told the New York Times.When he reached an employee in their 70s, Huang reportedly said the person was very old and that everyone was hoping they would drop dead.Huang allegedly told one employee that their mother should have "aborted" them and threatened another that he would rip off their head and “pee on your brain”.In another incident, he reportedly told a subordinate he would rip both their arms off and beat them to death with them.In a separate incident, Huang allegedly threw a water bottle at an executive during a fit of anger. He also reportedly told Jay Puri, Nvidia's then-executive vice-president of worldwide field operations: “I hope you get the flu and I hope it gets worse,” and “I hope you die and put us all out of our misery.”The report traced complaints about Huang's behaviour to at least the mid-2000s. Michael Winston, a former senior vice-president of human resources, threatened legal action against Nvidia in 2005 after alleging he was fired for objecting to Huang's conduct.During a two-day off-site meeting attended by around 50 employees, Huang allegedly made violent threats. “You have to do this, or I will rip your f–king heart out and stomp on it,” he reportedly said.Winston wrote in notes at the time that Huang “thinks he can get away with anything” and that employees were “terrorized” and asking him to intervene.Winston said he confronted Huang and warned him that his behaviour had “crossed the line” and could expose the company to lawsuits. Huang allegedly described the treatment as a “rite of passage” for employees and added: “It has good entertainment value,” according to the report.Winston was fired that November. Huang reportedly told him he was “not a good fit” and threatened to ensure he would never work again if he sued the company.Winston later filed a formal complaint with California's Department of Fair Employment and Housing and drafted a lawsuit. He reached a confidential settlement with Nvidia for $1 million before the lawsuit was filed. Winston died earlier this year.Six current and former employees told the New York Times that Huang's management style had created a workplace culture they compared to Stockholm syndrome, in which hostages develop an emotional bond with their abusers.As Nvidia grew and its employees became wealthy, Huang reportedly told groups of subordinates that money alone was no longer enough to motivate them and that he needed to humiliate them.The report also said some executives adopted similar behaviour. Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, who works in marketing at Nvidia and effectively served as his de facto chief of staff, reportedly used terms such as “dead-face” for employees who remained expressionless after being reprimanded in meetings.She also allegedly called employees “goldfish” if they could not remember something, according to the Wall Street Journal.Despite the accounts of his management style, Huang retained support among many employees. More than 200,000 people have signed an online petition calling for his reinstatement as CEO.Nvidia's board has not supported the idea. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who was herself reportedly belittled by Huang during a company meeting, urged employees to “move forward” during the first all-hands meeting held without him, according to sources cited in the report.
Article Summary: Report details allegations of repeated humiliation, verbal abuse and threats against employees by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang reportedly told one employee that their mother should have "aborted" them and threatened another that he would rip off their head and “pee on your brain”

Article Title: China bars new red-chip firms from offshore listings without shifting base
Article Text:
China's securities regulator is tightening overseas listing rules for new red-chip firms, a move that could delay IPOs and affect Hong Kong's fundraising market

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

China's securities regulator has told law firms that it will not approve overseas listing plans by red-chip companies set up after March 2023 unless they shift their domicile to mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move tightens Beijing's oversight of offshore fundraising and could affect Chinese companies planning to list in Hong Kong and New York.The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) conveyed the guidance to law firm representatives in recent days, the people said. They declined to be identified because the regulatory discussions were confidential, news agency Reuters reported.Red-chip companies are incorporated overseas, often in tax havens, but control businesses and assets in China through equity ownership or contractual arrangements. The structure has been popular among Chinese startups, particularly technology firms, seeking access to foreign investors and deeper capital markets.China's oversight of red-chip companies has gradually increased. Before March 2023, Chinese firms using overseas holding structures to raise funds abroad did not require regulatory approval.That changed with the introduction of new offshore listing rules in March 2023.In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those established after the rules came into effect.Despite the warning, some companies planning IPOs and their advisers continued to seek approval for overseas listings without dismantling their existing structures or shifting their domicile to China, one of the people said.Most failed to convince the regulator that retaining a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.The move comes as China and the US compete for an edge in technology, particularly in artificial intelligence and semiconductors. Chinese authorities have stepped up scrutiny of technology, data and capital flowing outside the country.
Article Summary: China's securities regulator has told law firms that it will not approve overseas listing plans by red-chip companies set up after March 2023. The move tightens Beijing's oversight of offshore fundraising and could affect Chinese companies planning to list in Hong Kong and New York. Red- chip companies are incorporated overseas, often in tax havens, but control businesses and assets in China.

Article Title: Water, power, noise: Anthropic's first Australia data centre faces major local opposition
Article Text:
Anthropic's first Australian data centre faces strong local opposition, with 595 of nearly 600 public submissions objecting to the project or seeking a delay

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic's first data centre project in Australia has faced overwhelming opposition from local residents, with 595 of nearly 600 public submissions either objecting to the development or seeking a delay over environmental concerns. The proposed Western Downs Digital Park, located about 250 km west of Brisbane, has Anthropic as its anchor tenant and is being developed by Zerra DC, news agency Reuters reported.Only two submissions supported the project, while one was neutral, according to a filing on the proposed development. The objections largely focused on concerns over water use, electricity demand, noise, road damage from construction traffic and pressure on housing.The proposed facility is planned on farmland, away from suburban areas. However, its planned computing load of 1.44 gigawatts would make it one of Australia's biggest data centres. About one-third of the submissions came from people living within 200 km of the site, the filing said.A Zerra spokesperson said the developer took the submissions seriously, adding that they "reinforce that people want a greater say in how the project develops".The company said it was expanding its community engagement and planned to report on changes sought by the public. Anthropic declined to comment.The timeline of submissions also showed a rise in opposition after Anthropic was named as the project's tenant on September 15. The project had received five objections in a month before the announcement, while the remaining submissions came in between September 15 and November 11, when the local government stopped accepting them.The opposition comes amid growing concerns among communities about the rapid expansion of data centres, often described as AI factories, around the world. The boom in data centre infrastructure has been valued at $7 trillion by 2030 by McKinsey.
Article Summary: Anthropic's first Australian data centre faces strong local opposition. 595 of nearly 600 public submissions objecting to the project or seeking a delay. Only two submissions supported the project, while one was neutral. The proposed facility is planned on farmland, away from suburban areas.

Article Title: How Claude propelled Anthropic start-up to become a $1.76 trillion giant in 5 years
Article Text:
Anthropic Claude AI Down: Users Report Access Issues With Claude Chatbot And Claude Code

From OpenAI employees to AI industry challenger

Why investors are watching Anthropic

A first for the AI industry

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind chatbot Claude, has reached a valuation of roughly $1.76 trillion following its stock market debut on Nasdaq on Thursday. Founded just five years ago by former OpenAI employees, the company has made one of the fastest journeys from start-up to public listing, riding growing demand for AI technology and investor enthusiasm for the sector.The company's shares were priced at $83 each before trading began. They surged to $111.53 in the initial hours, taking its market value close to $2 trillion, before settling at $97.17 by the end of the session. The closing price represented a gain of roughly 17% over the allocation price.According to the BBC, Anthropic's listing is a crucial test for the AI industry, which has attracted enormous investment amid questions about whether the technology can justify the money being spent on it.Anthropic was founded five years ago by seven former OpenAI employees, led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei. The company has since become one of the prominent names in the AI industry, largely through its chatbot Claude.Its rise has coincided with major advances in computing power and related technology. These developments have made it possible to process far larger amounts of data and build AI chatbots that can simulate human conversations.Such tools can also perform tasks including software coding, digital image generation and internet searches. This has opened up new ways of using computers and fuelled demand for AI products.Anthropic's rapid journey from start-up to stock market listing reflects the growing interest in this technology. Its public debut also gives the company access to a wider pool of investors as it looks to finance its expansion.Anthropic's listing comes amid an unprecedented wave of spending on AI. More than $1 trillion was spent in the last year alone by a handful of major technology companies to build the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI systems.The scale of investment has raised concerns about a possible financial bubble. The industry faces several challenges, including growing competition from cheaper AI models and shortages of expensive computer chips needed to run the technology.The US Federal Reserve has also flagged concerns about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures. Its October meeting minutes also pointed to the concentration of AI exposure among a small number of companies.Anthropic's public listing could help it raise additional funds to meet the high costs of developing AI. Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC, "AI is financially demanding," adding that public markets open up access to more funding.As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic is entering a market where investors have few direct comparisons. Its shares could see significant fluctuations as the market assesses its prospects, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.The initial excitement around a public listing may not last, he said, pointing to the experience of Elon Musk-led SpaceX. Its shares rose about 10% on the first day of trading, taking its valuation to a record $2.2 trillion. However, they fell below their debut price within a month and have mostly declined further since.Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said: "There's no obvious peer to compare it to."Anthropic's co-founder and chief executive Dario Amodei has also been vocal about the risks posed by AI, including the possibility of a threat to human existence. The company has called for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safeguards, even as it pursues rapid growth.Reuters reported that Anthropic's market debut came as technology stocks faced pressure, with the Nasdaq Composite Index falling nearly 2.3% on Thursday. Alphabet shares dropped 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.The company's performance will now be closely watched as investors assess whether its growth prospects can justify its enormous valuation.
Article Summary: Anthropic, the company behind chatbot Claude, has reached a valuation of roughly $1.76 trillion. Founded just five years ago by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic has made one of the fastest journeys from start-up to public listing. Its listing comes amid an unprecedented wave of spending on AI.

Article Title: Anthropic's IPO: Will the record listing stop the AI bubble from bursting
Article Text:
Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, around 34% above their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

Can the AI boom justify its valuations?

Safety concerns and public backlash

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The next test for AI stocks

Five years after emerging as a startup founded by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic has made history with the biggest public stock offering ever. Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, around 34% above their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83, before closing at $97.17, up 17.07%.The company raised $81.31 billion through the offering, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion fundraising haul. Its valuation briefly crossed $2 trillion during the first few minutes of trading before settling at around $1.75 trillion at the close.However, the strong debut did little to lift sentiment across the broader technology sector. US stocks came under pressure on Thursday, while Anthropic shares fell around 6% in premarket trading on Friday, slipping to $91.24.According to Reuters, the decline brought Anthropic's fully diluted valuation to around $1.7 trillion, while its market capitalisation based on shares outstanding stood at approximately $1.2 trillion.Anthropic's IPO is significant because it gives public market investors an opportunity to invest directly in an AI developer, rather than companies supplying the chips, computing infrastructure and data centres powering the technology."The reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," Fiona Cincotta from StoneX told BBC.She said previous offerings had largely involved other parts of the AI ecosystem, including semiconductor and data centre companies, while Anthropic's listing allows investors to access the AI provider itself.The offering is also expected to serve as a valuation benchmark for the wider AI industry. Its performance could influence investor sentiment towards other major players, including OpenAI, which has indicated that it could go public next year.Despite the strong demand, questions remain over whether AI companies can generate enough revenue to justify the enormous sums being invested in the technology.At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".However, the economics of the AI boom remain contentious. Companies are spending heavily on chips, data centres, computing power and talent, with some AI employees commanding annual salaries exceeding $100 million.There are also concerns about revenue concentration. Around a quarter of Anthropic's revenue reportedly comes from a handful of companies, including Google and Amazon, while the US accounts for roughly two-thirds of its revenue.The industry also has a growing network of circular financing arrangements, with companies investing in AI developers while simultaneously supplying them with chips and computing infrastructure or buying their products."Anthropic’s IPO attracted strong investor demand, with the stock opening 34% above its IPO price and closing 17% higher. However, the broader AI and technology stocks came under pressure, highlighting that a successful listing does not automatically lift the wider sector. The broader market was already under strain, and investors are reassessing valuations and the amount of capital flowing into AI," Prateek Gupta, Head of Business at Mudrex, told TOI. ""The listing also opens a new route for retail investors to access a company previously available largely through private markets. However, sustained performance will depend on business fundamentals and the ability to meet growth expectations. Investors should look beyond the initial rally and focus on valuation and long-term potential," Gupta added.Anthropic was founded by seven former OpenAI employees, including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, over differences in their approach to AI development. The company sought to place greater emphasis on safety while building increasingly powerful AI systems.However, its rapid expansion has raised questions about whether its development pace matches its stated commitment to responsible AI.In an interview with CNBC, Amodei compared the rapid development of AI, partly driven by advanced models helping build improved versions of themselves, to allowing a driver to increase speed from 60 miles per hour to 200 miles per hour."What we've done with pacing is essentially said, 'Look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely,'" he said. "And the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way."He has also warned that AI could enable biological weapons development, mass surveillance and authoritarianism, while potentially displacing millions of white-collar workers.In its filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Anthropic devoted 93 pages to outlining potential business risks, including the possibility that advanced AI systems could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."The debate has also extended beyond the technology industry. Growing public opposition to data centres, concerns over energy and water consumption, and fears of job losses have made AI development an increasingly contentious political issue in the US.Despite these concerns, investor enthusiasm remains strong. Orders for Anthropic shares reportedly exceeded the number available by more than six times, reflecting the fear of missing out on one of the biggest technology investment opportunities.However, a strong first-day performance does not necessarily guarantee long-term gains. SpaceX shares, for instance, initially rose nearly 70% from their IPO price of $135 to $225 before falling back to around $145, according to the figures cited in the BBC report.Some investors believe Anthropic's listing could reignite enthusiasm for AI stocks."Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investor Passion Capital, told BBC. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."Cincotta, meanwhile, believes the listing could have implications far beyond Anthropic, providing a benchmark for valuations across the AI industry.
Article Summary: Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17, up 17.07%. The company raised $81.31 billion through the offering, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion fundraising haul. Its valuation briefly crossed $2 trillion during the first few minutes of trading before settling at around $1.75 trillion.

Article Title: What's next for Anthropic shares - will it boom or pop?
Article Text:
Anthropic's record-breaking IPO raises questions over the sustainability of the AI boom as costs, regulation and safety concerns loom

Revenue is soaring, but so are costs

Data centres and regulation could weigh on shares

Anthropic's safety pledge faces scrutiny

What's next for Anthropic?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut has put the artificial intelligence company at the centre of a new debate over whether the AI boom can sustain its momentum. The maker of Claude chatbot ended its first day of trading on Thursday with a market valuation of around $1.75 trillion, after raising $81 billion in what was reported as the largest initial public offering ( IPO ) in history. But concerns over the industry's high spending, mounting risks and market volatility have raised questions about what lies ahead for its shares.The stock surged as much as 34% after trading began before closing about 17% above its IPO price at just over $97. The debut has made Anthropic one of the world's most valuable companies, but investors will now be watching whether the rally holds and how the company manages its growing costs, infrastructure investments and safety commitments.Why the AI market remains under pressureAnthropic's debut comes at a time when investor confidence in the broader AI industry remains unsettled. Major US stock indexes fell to seven-month lows on Thursday, while Asian markets also saw sharp declines in early trading on Friday.Despite the strong demand for Anthropic shares, analysts say its debut alone may not be enough to reassure investors about the long-term outlook for AI companies.Anthropic's rapid growth has been reflected in its revenue. According to its investor prospectus, the company generated $16.2 billion in revenue in the first six months of 2026, compared with $4.6 billion for the whole of 2025.However, the company has also reported substantial losses, including a reported $80 billion loss in the first half of 2026, largely attributed to a one-off charge. Its losses reportedly reached $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026.Anthropic is expected to spend heavily on infrastructure as it expands its AI operations. The company has plans to spend around $900 billion on data centre infrastructure over the next two decades, raising concerns about the scale of capital it may need to sustain its growth.The IPO provides the company with fresh capital for these investments, but analysts expect spending requirements and financing needs to remain a key concern for investors.Anthropic's expansion also comes amid growing opposition to AI infrastructure, particularly data centres, in the US. Protests against proposed data centre projects have gained momentum, with some municipalities and states voting for restrictions or bans.The company's growth is closely tied to investments in the infrastructure that powers AI tools such as Claude. A slowdown in data centre spending could have implications not just for Anthropic but also for the wider US economy.Regulatory scrutiny is another factor investors will be watching. Senior Democrats have signalled the possibility of tighter oversight of AI companies, citing concerns over the risks posed by advanced AI systems and the volatility that large AI IPOs could introduce into financial markets.Last month, Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, warning that the company's IPO “could inject extreme volatility and risk into the financial system, which threatens to undermine Americans' economic security.”Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is the company's president. The founders left OpenAI with a focus on prioritising safety in AI development.The company has repeatedly warned about the potential risks of advanced AI, even as it continues to develop increasingly powerful models. In a recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Anthropic devoted 93 pages to risk factors, including the possibility that advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”However, the company's safety commitments have also come under scrutiny. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, criticising the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI and arguing that the industry was moving too quickly.Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development and advocated greater coordination between companies and countries, along with independent evaluations of AI systems.Speaking at the Nasdaq opening bell on Thursday, Amodei said the company's “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us”.“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” he said.The tension between Anthropic's safety commitments and its commercial ambitions is likely to remain a key issue as the company enters public markets.Anthropic's performance in the coming months will depend on whether it can sustain its growth while managing rising infrastructure costs, regulatory scrutiny and concerns over the risks of advanced AI. The company's expansion is also tied to data centre investments, which have faced growing opposition in the US, with some municipalities and states voting for restrictions or bans.Regulatory oversight could add another layer of uncertainty. Senior Democrats have signalled the possibility of tighter scrutiny of AI companies over the risks posed by advanced AI systems and the volatility large IPOs could introduce into financial markets.Anthropic's safety commitments are also likely to remain under scrutiny. The company has repeatedly warned about the risks of advanced AI even as it continues to develop increasingly powerful models. CEO Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq opening bell on Thursday that the company's “most difficult safety work lies ahead of us”.The debut could also offer a signal for other AI firms planning to enter public markets. OpenAI, Anthropic's major rival, is expected to pursue an IPO in 2027. CEO Sam Altman said earlier this week that the company would go ahead with its IPO next year despite market volatility, adding, “There's been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.”
Article Summary: Anthropic's record-breaking IPO raises questions over the sustainability of the AI boom as costs, regulation and safety concerns loom. The maker of Claude chatbot ended its first day of trading on Thursday with a market valuation of around $1.75 trillion. The stock surged as much as 34% after trading began before closing about 17% above its IPO price at just over $97.

Article Title: Pentagon standoff, copyright lawsuit to AI safety concerns: 5 controversies that have put Anthropic under scrutiny
Article Text:
Anthropic's rapid rise has also brought a series of controversies.

The Pentagon standoff

$1.5 billion copyright settlement

Researcher’s ‘end of the world’ warning

Claude and the Venezuela raid

Changes to AI safety commitments

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anthropic has positioned itself as a safety-focused alternative in an increasingly competitive AI industry, building its reputation around responsible AI development and safeguards against potential misuse.Founded by former OpenAI employees, the company has repeatedly emphasised the need to ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain under human control.However, its rapid rise has also brought a series of controversies, ranging from copyright infringement allegations and disagreements with the US government over military applications to concerns about the existential risks of advanced AI.The most high-profile dispute erupted in February 2026, when Anthropic refused to remove restrictions preventing Claude from being used for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous lethal weapons. The US department of defence wanted broader authority to use the technology for what it called all lawful purposes.President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology, while defence secretary Pete Hegseth designated the company a national security supply-chain risk.Anthropic challenged the move in court. In September, a US appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s designation in a 2-1 decision, allowing the department to remove Claude from its systems and barring its use for Defence Department work.Anthropic said it disagreed with the appeals court ruling.Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle a class-action lawsuit brought by authors who accused it of downloading pirated books to train its AI models. A US court granted final approval in July 2026. The agreement covers more than 480,000 works allegedly obtained from pirate libraries, including Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror.The settlement followed a distinction drawn by a federal judge in 2025, which said that using copyrighted books to train AI models could qualify as fair use, but making and retaining copies of pirated books was not protected by that finding.However, the settlement did not establish that all AI training using copyrighted material is illegal.In September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that AI developers were racing towards self-improving superintelligence without adequately addressing the risks. Coxon, who said he had worked on pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, wrote that companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.He said people building the technology believed it could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. His comments were a warning about future risks, not evidence that existing AI systems have reached that level of capability. His resignation fuelled debate over whether AI development should slow until safeguards improve.Anthropic faced questions after reports that the US military had used Claude during the January 3 operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.The Wall Street Journal reported that the model was used in the mission, but Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Axios also reported its use during the active operation, while noting that the precise role was unclear.Anthropic said it could not comment on whether Claude had been used in a specific classified operation. The reports drew attention because the company’s restrictions on military use were already at the centre of its dispute with the Pentagon. The tasks Claude performed during the raid have not been publicly established.Anthropic’s safety policies have also come under scrutiny. In February 2026, it substantially rewrote its Responsible Scaling Policy, introducing Frontier Safety Roadmaps and regular risk reports. In July, it changed internal access rules for unredacted risk reports, requiring them to be shared with at least 200 employees rather than all staff with regular security clearance.In October, the company retired a roadmap goal for systematic oversight of training data to assess alignment with Claude’s Constitution. Anthropic said existing reviews were already identifying the issues such checks were designed to catch, and that a later sample review found no additional problems. It said it would reconsider which goals were most effective for alignment.
Article Summary: Anthropic has positioned itself as a safety-focused alternative in an increasingly competitive AI industry. The company has repeatedly emphasised the need to ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain under human control. Its rapid rise has also brought a series of controversies, ranging from copyright infringement allegations and disagreements with the US government over military applications.

Article Title: 1.14 lakh startups generate more than 12 lakh jobs in India: Finance ministry
Article Text:
Finance Ministry

NEW DELHI: More than 1.14 lakh startups in India have created over 12 lakh jobs so far, the finance ministry said in its latest review of the Indian economy.In the report titled, ‘The Indian Economy: A Review January 2024’, the Department of Economic Affairs said that the 1.14 lakh startups recognised by the government under the 'Startup India initiative’ created more than 12 lakh jobs (as of October 2023).The state-owned e-commerce platform Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) clocked more than 63 lakh transactions till November 2023, the document read.Despite facing global challenges in 2023 like valuation issues, few IPOs, regulatory changes and macroeconomic and geopolitical trends, India remains the third largest tech start-up ecosystem globally, with over 950 tech startups founded last year.The cumulative funding for more than 31,000 tech start ups has exceeded $70 billion (from 2019 to 2023), according to a recent report by Nasscom in collaboration with Zinnov.“In 2023, despite facing global economic and regulatory challenges, Indian tech startups have prioritised the imperative of enhancing their business fundamentals, driving profitability and growth,” said Debjani Ghosh, President, Nasscom.“The proliferation of tech startups in tier 2 and 3 cities marks the ecosystem's resilience,” she added.Navigating 2024, tech startup founders expect to continue the revenue growth path with measured steps focusing on optimising expenditure and maximising profitability for B2B tech startups.Investments in deeptech will continue an upward trend in 2024. With generative AI (GenAI) acceleration, 70 per cent of start-up founders are embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in their solutions.As funding becomes scarce for the Indian startup ecosystem in general, the explosion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given a new lease of life to entrepreneurs and founders in the country, as the Centre extends support to the sector.
